1.2.2.2-f13.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Annals 16.18, uses 'erudito luxu' of Petronius, the elegantiae arbiter.

1.2.2.2-f2.accuracy_reason: Ecclesiasticus 37:34 in the Vulgate does read 'propter crapulam multi obierunt'. The note fairly calls the saying proverbial.

1.2.2.2-f3.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.140–144 describes a man who eats a whole boar alone and then takes an undigested peacock into the bath. Sudden death and dying without a will follow, so the note is right.

1.2.2.2-f33.accuracy_reason: Georgics 1.250–251 describes the antipodes, and the line reads 'illic sera rubens accendit lumina Vesper'. Burton's 'Illis' is indeed his change.

1.2.2.2-f35.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Verr. 2.5.26 says Verres was seldom seen 'non modo extra tectum, sed ne extra lectum quidem'. That is the source of the jingle.

1.2.2.2-f45.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.738–739 reads 'ille impiger hausit / spumantem pateram', said of Bitias at Dido's feast. There is no 'vino' in Virgil's text.

1.2.2.2-f74.accuracy_reason: Santorio's De statica medicina (Venice, 1614) taught regimen by weighing the body and what goes in and out of it. The identification is plausible and properly hedged ('almost certainly').

1.2.2.2-f75.accuracy_reason: Philippians 3:19 in the Vulgate reads 'quorum deus venter est'.
